Frostbite (Table 1)

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Burns
Although the volar portion of the hand may be more likely to be burned (because of tactical
use), the dorsal hand fares worse after burns and may be more vulnerable to subsequent
contracture because the skin is thinner and less fixed dorsally. Glabrous skin is bound by the
palmar fascia volarly.6
Frostbite
The hands and feet are affected in more than 90% of frostbite episodes that require
hospitalization.7

The resulting edema and eschar in the hand can compress neurovascular structures and

Joint stiffness after burn injuries occurs because of edema, fibrosis, and scar contracture.6
Electrical burns
The degree of tissue damage is related to the current, voltage, exposure time, and path of
the current.6
Low voltage is less than 1,000 volts; high voltage is more than 1,000 volts.6
Electrical burns often have associated thermal burns.
More substantial tissue damage may be observed deep to the entry point of the electrical
burn.8
Deep tissue damage and compartment swelling may lead to compartment syndrome.8

Alkali causes cellular dehydration and the saponification of adipose tissue.6

Mechanism of Injury
Frostbite occurs if prolonged cold exposure results in cellular damage and ischemia of
the skin. Skin freezes at -2°C (28.4°F).5 Extracellular and intracellular ice crystals, which
form at -6°C (21.2°F) to -15°C (5°F), cause cellular dehydration and mechanical damage.
Ischemia results from endothelial injury, thrombosis, and vasoconstriction. After
rewarming, microvascular emboli form, causing additional ischemic injury.6 Cytokine-
mediated and free–radical-mediated tissue damage also occurs after reperfusion.4

Patient factors (intoxicants, peripheral vascular disease, medications, psychiatric illness)9

Superficial partial-thickness burns cause blistering, are tender, and heal reliably.
Deep, partial-thickness burns also blister but may appear more mottled or white, with
sluggish capillary refill. If the skin does not heal by 3 weeks postinjury, deep, partial-

Frostbite
Recent studies have favored a simplified classification system.9
Superficial frostbite: pale plaques with surrounding erythema, swelling, clear or milky
blisters, deforms easily
Deep frostbite: hemorrhagic blisters, loss of skin, mottled and indurated tissue, loss of
sensation
Nonsurgical Management
The treatment goals for burns and frostbite are to address the associated medical conditions
and injuries, prevent infection, maintain tissue viability, decrease pain, maintain motion, and
preserve function. Transfer to a burn center may be considered.

Immediate cool water applied to the burned skin

Fingertip and Nail Bed Injuries
Pathophysiology and Pathoanatomy
Overview
Nail bed lacerations
Distal phalanx fractures
Fingertip amputations
Epidemiology

Epidemiology
Fingertip and nail bed injuries are some of the most common hand injuries that occur in
children and adults. In children, these injuries most often result from a crush
mechanism; in adults, lacerations are the most common mechanism of fingertip injury.18
In a study of 455 young children treated for a hand injury, fingertip injuries were the
most common type of hand injury, with the long fingertip most frequently injured.19
Distal phalanx fractures frequently occur in combination with fingertip injuries. Tuft
fractures are the most common fracture type in children and adults. Diaphyseal distal
phalanx fractures also occur in both age groups. In children, the physis of the distal
phalanx is weaker than the extensor tendon insertion, making children susceptible to
physeal fractures of the distal phalanx (Seymour fractures). Alternatively, adults are
more prone to mallet (bony or tendinous) injuries, in which the extensor mechanism
avulses off the distal phalanx with or without a piece of bone.20

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Figure 2 shows the sagittal and cross-sectional anatomy of the fingertip. The fingernail,
also referred to as the nail plate, is adherent to the underlying nail bed, which sits on the
dorsal surface of the distal phalanx. The nail bed has two sections: the sterile matrix and
the germinal matrix. The sterile matrix is distal to the lunula, which is the white region
distal to the nail fold. The germinal matrix consists of the floor of the nail fold
(eponychium) and is the tissue that produces the nail plate. The rate of nail growth is
approximately 0.1 mm per day.21 The extensor tendon inserts on the distal phalanx just
proximal to the germinal matrix. The tissue proximal to the nail plate is the eponychium,
the tissue on the radial and ulnar aspects of the nail plate is the paronychium, and the
tissue distal to the nail plate (at the tip of the digit) is the hyponychium. The pad of the
digit (palmar to the distal phalanx) is the pulp. The pulp consists of subcutaneous fat,
branches of the digital arteries and digital nerves, and septae (which tether the skin to
the bone).22 The flexor tendon inserts onto the proximal palmar aspect of the distal
phalanx. In pediatric patients, the physis of the distal phalanx is located at the proximal
aspect of the bone.

Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patient History

Patient History
The initial history for all patients with a fingertip injury should include the mechanism of
injury, the time of injury, hand dominance, and occupation (if applicable). A complete
medical history should include immune status (diabetes mellitus, immune suppression
medication), history of vasospasm (eg, Raynaud syndrome), and the use of
vasoconstrictive agents (caffeine, tobacco, cocaine, methamphetamine). The most recent
tetanus vaccination should be documented. If the injury resulted from an animal bite,
the type of animal, and the vaccination status of the animal also should be documented
if known. The patient history also should note whether the patient has received oral,
intramuscular, or intravenous antibiotic agents.
Physical Examination
During the examination of an injured fingertip, the clinician should document the following:
Presence or absence of a distal phalanx fracture (based on physical examination and
radiographs)
Soft-tissue coverage over the bone (and whether the bone is exposed in the wound)
Presence or absence of a subungual hematoma (if applicable)
Status of the nail plate (intact, absent, or partially present)
Location of the laceration(s) using the anatomic terms for the fingertip
Orientation of the laceration(s) (Figure 3)

Nailbed Laceration
Some debate exists about the treatment of patients with a subungual hematoma and
presumed nail bed laceration. Proposed treatment options include nail plate removal and
suture repair of the nail bed, nail plate removal and skin adhesive repair of the nailbed, and
nail plate trephination; however, inadequate experimental evidence is available to support any
treatment option over the natural history of unmanaged subungual hematoma.28
Fehrenbacher and Blackburn28 proposed the following treatment algorithm:
Patients with a subungual hematoma who have an intact and adherent nail plate (with or
without a nondisplaced or minimally displaced distal phalanx fracture) are treated via
observation or trephination alone.
Patients with a proximal distal phalanx fracture involving the germinal matrix, a displaced
distal phalanx fracture requiring surgical stabilization, and/or a nail plate injury or floating
nail are treated via removal of the remaining nail plate and repair of the nail bed.

Bony Mallet Fracture

Bony Mallet Fracture
Closed extensor tendon avulsion fractures (bony mallet fractures) with a congruent
distal phalangeal joint may be managed via splint immobilization. Full-time distal
interphalangeal joint extension splint immobilization typically is recommended for 6 to 8
weeks, followed by a period of night splinting. Proximal interphalangeal joint motion
should be initiated immediately, with the caveat that patients who have a compensatory
swan neck deformity may require anti-swanning splint immobilization at the proximal
interphalangeal joint. Surgeons must instruct the patient to take care to avoid skin
complications from pressure and moisture accumulation under the splint. Early referral
to hand therapy may be helpful for splint fabrication and management.23,29 Closed
extensor tendon avulsion injuries (tendinous mallet injuries) may be managed in a
similar fashion29 (Figure 5).

Seymour Fracture

Seymour Fracture
Successful management of Seymour fractures begins with prompt recognition of the
injury. A displaced distal phalanx physeal fracture may be associated with a proximal nail
bed injury, which may be considered an open fracture. Classically, a flexed posture to
the distal phalanx will be observed, and the proximal nail plate will be superficial to the
eponychium (Figure 6). A lateral radiograph is essential in making the diagnosis (Figure
7). Closed injuries may be managed with the use of a splint, with careful follow-up to
ensure reduction is maintained.23 Often, this injury is an open injury, and surgical
management is appropriate.

Techniques and Procedures
Nailbed Repair

Nailbed Repair
Most nailbed injuries can be repaired under a digital block in the emergency department
or an office procedure room. A digital tourniquet may be helpful for improved
hemostasis and visualization if local anesthetic with epinephrine is not used; however,
care must be taken to remove the tourniquet at the completion of the procedure as a
safety check. The remaining nail plate is removed, and the nail bed laceration and any
associated distal phalanx fracture are irrigated gently and débrided. Care should be
taken to avoid removing excessive nail bed tissue; removal of excessive tissue may result
in tension on the nail bed repair. Longitudinal or slightly oblique incisions on the radial
and ulnar aspect of the eponychial fold may be used to retract the nail fold and débride
and repair of the proximal nail bed. The nail bed laceration is repaired with the use of 6-
0 chromic suture (or other small-caliber, absorbable suture) or with the use of tissue
adhesive (eg, 2-octyl cyanoacrylate).31 If adhesive is used, it should be allowed to dry
completely before the remaining nail plate or a piece a nonadherent gauze is placed
under the eponychial fold. A splint may be applied for soft-tissue protection and fracture
care.

Seymour Fracture

Seymour Fracture
Because this fracture is a pediatric injury, general anesthesia typically is used. The nail
plate is removed, after which the nail bed laceration and fracture site often are visible. If
necessary, longitudinal incisions on the radial and ulnar aspect of the eponychial fold
may be used to retract the nail fold and allow access to the proximal nail bed. Flexion of
the fingertip through the fracture allows the interposed tissue to be removed from the
fracture site and the fracture to be thoroughly irrigated (Figure 10). The fracture then is
reduced via extension and stabilized with the use of a retrograde, longitudinal 0.035-inch
Kirschner wire placed across the fracture and the distal interphalangeal joint. The
incisions (if made) and nail bed laceration are repaired with the use of 6-0 chromic or
plain gut suture. The avulsed nail plate or a piece of nonadherent gauze may be placed
under the eponychial fold. The Kirschner wire and fracture are protected in a short arm
splint or cast until the wire is removed at 3 to 4 weeks postoperatively20 (Video 2).

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The anatomic structures involved in injection and extravasation injuries are determined

Extravasation Injuries

Extraversion Injuries
The mechanism of injury of the extravasated fluid depends on whether the extravasate
is neutral, an irritant, or a vesicant. Concentration, volume, time of exposure, and
infusion pressure also influence the degree and extent of an extravasation injury.43
Irritants cause local inflammatory symptoms but are not toxic to the tissue. Vesicants
cause cell death and can cause substantial soft-tissue damage.43

High-Pressure Injection Injuries

High-Pressure Injection Injuries
Similar to extravasation injuries, the type of material injected, injection pressure,
volume, time of exposure, and location of injection are factors that determine the extent
and severity of an injury from a high-pressure injection. The pressure required to
penetrate human skin is 7 bar (100 psi). Spray guns, fuel injectors, and water guns
typically operate between 150 and 500 bar.44 Soft-tissue damage may result from the
mechanical trauma of the spray, distension and swelling of the soft tissues, compression
of neurovascular structures, toxicity of the injected substance, and inflammatory
response to the injection. Subsequent infection also can occur.42
Epinephrine Injections Into Digits

Epinephrine Injections Into Digits
Epinephrine causes vasoconstriction by acting on the vascular smooth muscle cells
through the alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors.45 If epinephrine-mediated vasoconstriction
is sufficiently severe and prolonged, the tip of the digit may be deprived of sufficient
blood flow for survival, and necrosis occurs; however, necrosis was not reported in 59
cases of high-dose epinephrine injections into digits (some unmanaged).39 In addition,
the typical dose of lidocaine with epinephrine used in local anesthesia (1:100,000) is safe
for use in digits.46 If desired, epinephrine effect may be reversed via phentolamine. This
is useful for inadvertent high-dose epinephrine injection because it obviates possible
prolonged digital neuropraxia (months). In general, phentolamine (2 to 5 mg) is
reconstituted in saline and injected in the same region epinephrine was injected.47

Techniques and Procedures
The Gault technique can be used in the early management of extravasation injuries. This
technique involves flushing the subcutaneous tissues to wash out the extravasated
material (Figure 21). The procedure is performed under a local anesthetic.
Hyaluronidase can be injected initially at the site of the extravasation. Next, multiple
puncture outflow tracts are made at the periphery of the area of extravasation, and
copious saline is infiltrated through the subcutaneous tissue.43

Severe extravasation injuries involving large volumes or vesicant extravasate may

Early surgical management often is a critical aspect of the management of high-pressure

Rehabilitation

Rehabilitation
Patients with injection or extravasation injuries benefit from a multidisciplinary team
approach. Acute and subacute care coordination among the surgical, medical, and
rehabilitation teams is paramount. Severe injuries may require long-term follow-up to
address pain management, rehabilitation, and the possible need for future
reconstructive surgical procedures.
